entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The 228 Incident was a 1947 uprising in Taiwan that took place on February 27, 1947, and ended on May 16, 1947. It was a pivotal event in Taiwanese history, marking the escalation of tensions between the ruling Kuomintang (KMT) government and the Taiwanese people. The incident began with a dispute over cigarette sales taxes and soon turned into a full-scale rebellion, with protesters demanding greater autonomy and an end to KMT rule. The event had significant consequences, including the deaths of thousands of Taiwanese and the eventual establishment of martial law in Taiwan.

The 228 Incident was a turning point in Taiwan's history, as it exposed the deep-seated grievances of the Taiwanese people against the KMT government. The incident was marked by widespread violence and human rights abuses, with both sides committing atrocities. The event ultimately led to the establishment of the Taiwanese democracy, as the people demanded greater freedoms and an end to authoritarian rule.

The 228 Incident has had a lasting impact on Taiwanese society and politics. It has been remembered as a symbol of resistance against oppressive government and a call for greater democracy and human rights. The incident has also been the subject of much controversy and debate, with some viewing it as a heroic struggle for independence and others seeing it as a violent uprising against a legitimate government.
